In that capacity he was involved in various high-level negotiations with political and military representatives of the warring factions, including negotiations to open the airport in Sarajevo, negotiations to evacuate JNA barracks in Sarajevo, negotiations to evacuate the JNA from Dubrovnik, and negotiations to implement the no-fly zone over Bosnia. In December 1992 General Wilson became the military adviser to Cyrus Vance, Lord Owen, and later Ambassador Stoltenberg at the international conference for the former Yugoslavia, where he also served as the UNPROFOR liaison officer to the conference. General Wilson's written evidence describes the deployment of United Nations military observers in Bosnia and the work they and he performed, observations relating to shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo by Bosnian Serb forces, descriptions of reports he received about ethnic cleansing in Eastern Bosnia, descriptions of negotiations in which he participated, and interactions he had with representatives of the various the parties engaged in the conflict, including Ratko Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Zivota Panic. His written evidence describes complaints by Lord Owen made directly to Bosnian Serb representatives during peace negotiations about -- complaints about ethnic cleansing and military operations directed against the civilian population. That concludes my summary, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Now, General Wilson, you were Chief of the United Nations Military Observers from March 1992 until December 1992. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what United Nations Military Observers were and what were their duties and responsibilities? What was the mandate that they had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The military observers in UNPROFOR were a group initially of some 75 officers drawn from different countries, I think about 20 different countries were represented. They were usually between the rank of captain and lieutenant colonel. Nearly all of them were professional officers, although some reserve officers may also have been represented. Their task was broadly to liaise with the parties in conflict, to participate in negotiations, to assist the parties to achieve agreements or to effect the exchange, perhaps, of prisoners of war or bodies that resulted from conflicts, and they were a source of information for the United Nations to find out what was going on in the area. The specific mandate of the UNPROFOR military observers was under the Vance Plan, was to deploy in areas of growing ethnic tension within Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was namely in the area of Bihac and also in Mostar. They were the only elements of UNPROFOR that had an operational task within Bosnia-Herzegovina when UNPROFOR was established in March 1992. The remainder of UNPROFOR's operational focus was in the UNPAs in Croatia. I think that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Wilson, as part of their duties and responsibilities, did they send daily reports to UNPROFOR headquarters and to you about what was happening in their areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They did. They were required to provide reports on two channels; one with the UN forces that they were supporting and one directly to my headquarters. Those reports were summarized and forwarded up the command chain to UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to direct your attention, General Wilson, to paragraph 73 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is 65 -- I'm sorry, that would be Exhibit number -- P137, and I would like to turn to page 15 of the e-court document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Specifically, I'd like to focus your attention about four lines from the bottom of that paragraph. It says, in part, and I'm going to -- it says: "On this occasion and later meetings in early June, I observed the relationship between Panic and Mladic, and it was clear that Mladic acted in a subordinate manner towards Panic. Panic actually forced the issue to hand over weapons -- handover of weapons on Mladic despite his strenuous objections." First of all, to be perfectly clear, who was Panic and what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Panic, as I understood, was the commander of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was the position of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Mladic was, or claimed at the time to be the commander of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber the circumstances under which you met General Panic in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We had been negotiating with the Bosnian Serb leadership and the Presidency to effect the evacuation of the JNA out of three barracks in Sarajevo. One barracks was successfully evacuated. The second barracks, the largest of the three, was the Marshal Tito barracks, and they were lengthy and complicated negotiations. Essentially what the JNA represented at those negotiations was to effect the evacuation at whatever cost. The Presidency's position was to extract as many concessions as they could from the Serb leadership before the evacuation was allowed. The Bosnian military position or the Bosnian Serb position was that the evacuation should be effected without any concessions being made at all. It became quite clear that the Presidency was not going to assist in the evacuation unless there were significant concessions made; namely, the handover of weapons which they believed belonged to them. General Mladic's position was that he was adamantly against such a handover. General Panic arrived from Belgrade to take part in the negotiations. I transported him from the Lukavica barracks across to the PTT building to participate in those negotiations and later to take him to Marshal Tito barracks so he could brief the commander there on the results of those negotiations. I also transported him back to Lukavica barracks, and on the occasion that I picked him up at Lukavica barracks and also when I delivered him back there, I was able to see the interaction between Generals Panic and Mladic. I was also aware that General Panic had made it clear in the negotiations that the JNA was prepared to hand over weapons to effect the evacuation, despite General Mladic's objections, and it was General Panic's position that prevailed in the end. The weapons were handed over, and General Mladic had to accept that situation. I noted in the interaction between General Mladic and General Panic that there was a clear superior and subordinate interaction between the two, the paying of military compliments. The way that General Mladic addressed General Panic, to me, made it quite clear that General Mladic was subordinate to General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn -- let me turn, then, General Wilson, when you say he was subordinate, your statement says he acted in a subordinate manner towards Panic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does. And I'm saying there that it was -- collectively his actions, the way they talked, the demeanor of both men, made it clear to me that he was acting in a subordinate manner to a superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to a different area and that -- I want to just, first of all, focus on where your headquarters were located, General Wilson. I'll just summarize this. I'd like you just to affirm that this is the case. Initially, you had temporary headquarters in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo, and in early April 1992, UNPROFOR headquarters relocated from the Holiday Inn to the PTT building in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the PTT building is in the urban area of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you remained in -- personally remained in Sarajevo until the 24th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You relocated, then, in late July to -- strike that. You remained in day-to-day control of the United Nations Military Observers until the 15th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General Wilson, while you remained in Sarajevo, did you have -- did you personally observe the shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I did observe the shelling of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how did you have an opportunity to observe that shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I was able -- initially I was residing in an apartment block in Sarajevo when the war broke out and the fighting was in my immediate vicinity. It was very heavy and sustained fighting. After I had relocated my accommodation to the PTT building, it was quite possible from the PTT building, which is a glass and aluminum structure and quite a tall building, to be able to observe the vast majority of the area -- of the Sarajevo urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to P137, if I could turn to page 11 of the e-court document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to paragraph 47. I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 47 of your statement. In paragraph 47 of your statement, General Wilson, you say that: "The Presidency troops did not have a great number of heavy weapons." You saw 81 millimetre motors and you describe -- let me ask you this: Can you describe the disparity in terms of the calibre of weapons, heavy weapons, between the Presidency forces and the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. It was thought at the time that -- and I had seen certainly map evidence to support this, that the Presidency -- wrong, that the Serbian military forces around Sarajevo had something in the vicinity of 200 artillery and mortar barrels that they could direct at the city. In terms of military power, this is a significant capability. In addition to that, they also had a large number of other weapons, such as anti-aircraft weapons which they were able to use in a ground role, a direct-fire role. Additionally they had armoured forces that could also deploy their main armament to engage targets in the city. The Presidency forces, as indicated in my statement, had a very small number of what I'd describe as heavy weapons. That's mortars or artillery pieces. I only saw two or three tanks that were in their possession. There was a significant disparity in the weight of fire that both sides could bring to bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Wilson, did you have occasion to see a mobile mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I did. I was observing one day from the -- high up on the PTT building, on the road which ran down to the city. I saw a truck with an 81 millimetre mortar mounted on the back. It was firing a short number of rounds, two or three rounds, out, I presume, against the Serbian military forces and it was then quickly redeploying. Now, the reaction to this fire was a return of artillery fire by the Bosnian Serb forces. It was a significant return of fire involving very heavy calibre artillery, I assess probably 150-millimetre artillery, plus 120-millimetre artillery. There were a large number of rounds which were fired back into what was a civilian area. These rounds hit certainly the road area but also a large number of rounds hit surrounding accommodation buildings causing significant damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could turn your attention, General Wilson, to paragraph 53 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's page 12 of the e-court document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Paragraph 53 of your statement should appear in front of you. It says: "General shelling and sniping in Sarajevo was such a common occurrence that they were not investigated. It became part of the day-to-day reality in Sarajevo." From your perspective as a career military officer, can you provide the Trial Chamber with your general observations about both shelling and sniping in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can. For a period of approximately six weeks prior to the time that I left Sarajevo at the end of June, shelling and sniping within Sarajevo was a daily event. It was -- on most days for that six weeks, it was very heavy. It was directed virtually at the whole of the city, so it was widespread. It was intense for, on some days, 16 hours. It started at 5.00 in the morning and go through until 11.00 at night. It was indiscriminate, in my view, in that it engaged widely dispersed targets that had no clear military value to them. On other occasions the artillery was clearly in support of ground assaults taking place. But for the most part, the artillery being directed into the city was, in my view, indiscriminate, widespread, and did not take account of the fact that civilians were residing in the area. "Sniping" is a term, I think, which can be interpreted in a number of different ways. The pure technical description of a sniper is a highly trained marksman who can engage a target at a thousand or 1.200 metres with a great degree of accuracy. The local people in the former Yugoslavia tended to describe an individual with a weapon firing as a sniper. I think in the case of Sarajevo people were really talking about individual riflemen who were engaging targets within the city. Once again, this was common, particularly down in the downtown area, where individuals would engage, quite often civilians travelling on trams or as pedestrians in the street. On numerous occasions, to fulfil my UN responsibilities, I was required to go downtown and the vehicle in which I travelled, I would say, 70 or 80 per cent of the time, was engaged by this small-arms fire. It was too dangerous to go down to the city in other than an armoured vehicle. And the people of Sarajevo lived in this environment certainly for the six weeks that I was in Sarajevo, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Wilson, now I want to focus your attention on a slightly different topic, and that is, what information about what was happening in Bosnia and what was happening in Sarajevo was available to you while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the most important preamble here is that most international media left Sarajevo in mid-May when the war broke out and didn't return until sometime in early June. So, to the best of my knowledge, the only media in the city at that time were former Yugoslavia republic reporters. In the PTT we had the facility to be able to translate the written media that was produced in the city, and when we had electricity, we were able to watch the local Sarajevo TV. Additional to that, from Sarajevo headquarters we received regular operational reports which indicated their knowledge of what was happening in Sarajevo, and we also received daily media summaries in written form which summarized what was happening in the media in the former Yugoslavia and in the international written media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "summaries from the media from the former Yugoslavia," did that include summaries of media from Belgrade, from Zagreb, and from other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, mainly, to my memory, Zagreb and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did those media summaries relate in respect of, one, the events in Sarajevo, specifically shelling and sniping; and, two, events in Bosnia that related to ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. I made --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question posed is vague as to time, and if we could have a bit for focus, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the first question that I asked General Wilson and I've been directing my questions to him about deal with the time period he was in Sarajevo. I intend to explore with him later the media coverage that was available when he was in Belgrade, but these questions and the last question is to be understood as relating to the time he was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we take those two questions one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, General Wilson, in the media summaries that were coming from the former Yugoslavia, including those from Belgrade and those from Zagreb, what information was available and what was reported about the shelling and sniping that was occurring in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The media summaries indicated that there was extensive coverage of the military attacks against the city, both in the form of artillery and also small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was that being reported in the Belgrade press, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in respect of other events in Bosnia, ethnic cleansing, for example, focusing on the Belgrade media reports that you were receiving, was there any reference to the practice of ethnic cleansing in the events on the ground relating to it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, it certainly would not be addressed as that and, indeed, the Belgrade media would tend to focus on the Serb refugees that were generated by the war. I have no recollection of a detailed account of ethnic cleansing per se or any great mention of the number of Muslim or Croat refugees that had been created by the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in terms of the television coverage of events that were occurring in Sarajevo while you were in Sarajevo, could you describe what that coverage consisted of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The television coverage was provided by Sarajevo Television. It was graphic footage of attacks against civilians with, in the case of an attack on the 27th of May against a bread line, continual replaying of quite graphic shots of casualties, wounded. This sort of coverage would go on for hours, repetition of that sort of scenery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And while you were with UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, did you get coverage from the international media, CNN, SkyNews, BBC, and the like?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: After some time we were able to receive CNN, BBC news, by satellite transmission, but it took us some couple of weeks after UNPROFOR headquarters relocated to Belgrade before my headquarters was able to have this facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what do you recall the international media was broadcasting in respect of the events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In my view, they were fairly accurately representing what was taking place there. It was also quite clear that what was happening in the former Yugoslavia was the lead item on the news virtually around the world for that time and for many months after.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say what was happening -- your evidence was "in my view they were fairly accurately representing what was taking place there," what was it they were showing on the video -- on the television that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the timeframe we're talking about, but until the international media were able to get back into the city, they were reliant on other people, I presume, for TV footage. But my recollection is that there were certainly statements by journalists as to what was happening, and later when the cameras were able to get into the city, there was actual footage of shelling, civilian casualties, damage being caused to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General Wilson, you relocated from Sarajevo on the 24th of June. You went to Belgrade, and you remained in Belgrade until late July 1992. During that period of time, General Wilson, did you have -- did you continue to receive media compilations from UNPROFOR headquarters which included reports of -- summaries of the media throughout the former Yugoslavia, as well as international media publications?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were those summaries similar to the summaries that you've described in your previous -- in your earlier testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Belgrade, was there television coverage about what was happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, there was, but I don't speak Serbo-Croat so the exact content of them, I don't know. But certainly the visual content seemed to suggest that there was very heavy fighting going on down in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was there television coverage through CNN and through BBC and SkyNews that was being received in Belgrade while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We had the facility for that. I don't know whether the local people there did or did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell me, General Wilson, what was your impression about the people of Belgrade insofar as being informed about what was happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll have to object to that question. The impression of the people of Belgrade, the entire city of Belgrade, I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll reframe the question. I don't mean the entire people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General Wilson. In terms of the people with whom you had contact -- strike that. Did you have contact with people in Belgrade, who, first of all, discussed the events with you in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I left Sarajevo and returned to Belgrade, I reoccupied my accommodation in the Yugoslav Hotel. Since I'd lived in that hotel for several months before going to Yugoslavia, I was quite well known there to the domestic staff and they were -- some of them spoke to me and asked me for my opinion as to the likely safety -- the safety of their relatives down in the city. They indicated that they had seen reports of what was happening in Sarajevo, and they were greatly concerned for the safety of their family down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. General Wilson, I want to change the topic. I want to fast-forward to the period when you acted as a military advisor to Cyrus Vance, Lord Owen, and Ambassador Stoltenberg at the ICFY negotiations. In your trial testimony you were asked questions about Lord Owen and Lord Owen bringing to the attention of the Bosnian Serb leaders events that were taking place, ethnic cleansing and the like, and your testimony found at transcript pages 13080 to 13083, as well as 13110, you indicated, to put it succinctly, that Lord Owen spoke directly, bluntly, and non-diplomatically to Karadzic and others about what was happening in Bosnia. Do you recall your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did make that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what you weren't asked, and what I want to ask you about briefly about was the parties to the ICFY negotiations also included representatives from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, for example, Slobodan Milosevic, and the FRY foreign minister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Lord Owen express similar concerns to Slobodan Milosevic and FRY officials about events that were occurring in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and it was done in basically two forums, in one-on-one meetings, basically between General Milosevic and the co-chairman. The co-chairman would generally raise whatever issue was paramount at that time. It might be the cutting off of electricity or water to the city. It might be the provision of emergency aid. It could be the intensity of military action against the city at that time. At various stages they would use a different approach with General Milosevic. In the early days they would ask for his support and intervention, and he would usually respond that he would try and use his influence, but he had limited influence over the Bosnian Serb leadership. Later they would become more direct and ask that he take urgent action. In many cases he would disassociate himself with the actions of the Bosnian Serbs. He would agree that their actions were inappropriate, but he would claim that he had no authority, no way of influencing them. There's a second forum in which he would be -- the co-chairman would be negotiating with the Bosnian Serb leadership, mainly Karadzic, Milosevic, maybe Plavsic, and President Milosevic would be present and it would not be possible to progress the negotiations because the Presidency were refusing to participate until some military or humanitarian crisis was resolved. This was quite a common event and was quite common for Lord Owen to speak very directly to the participants there about what was happening and to demand their intervention and to point out to them the inappropriateness of this conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of conduct was he specifically describing when he was directing his comments to Milosevic and describing -- and to Karadzic and other participants in the ICFY negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were many of these meetings and, of course, many such discussions, but to summarize, it would certainly deal with the nature of military action being conducted in Bosnia in general and in Sarajevo in particular, but also be matters of a humanitarian nature and specifically about the conduct of ethnic cleansing which continued right through my period with the ICFY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just to follow up, in your answer, General Wilson, you said: "There were many of these meetings, and, of course, many such discussions, but to summarize to would certainly deal with the nature of the military action being conducted in Bosnia in general and in Sarajevo ..." Did he go -- what did he say about the nature of the military action being conducted in Bosnia and in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, it certainly depends upon the event or the particular time, but typically -- I can quote an example. The turning on and turning off of electricity -- I'm sorry, you asked for military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. Shelling, I think, is a particularly good example because shelling tended to fluctuate during 1993. It continued through 1993 but was more intense at some times rather than others, and Lord Owen would be asking for moderation of artillery fire being directed at the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, let me direct your attention, General Wilson, to Prosecution Exhibit P146.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have that pulled up on the screen, and I would like to go to page 1, the bottom of page 1, of that particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The paragraph, which is paragraph 4, I want to direction your attention to, is paragraph 4 and it carries over to page 2 as well. So let me just read that part of what is on paragraph 4: "In regard to the proposal of opening Sarajevo airport, the General said the airport was the most practical resupply route for humanitarian assistance." I'm sorry, I'm reading from the wrong paragraph. Let me go back to paragraph 3: "International military intervention could only bring catastrophe on Sarajevo as, in a military option, Sarajevo would be leveled." Can you just explain what that paragraph -- the context of that paragraph, General Wilson?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: This was a meeting that we had with General Plavsic to talk about the possibility of opening the airport for the delivery of assistance of humanitarian aid. This was an aside. At that time there was some discussion in the international media that some of the western European nations might be prepared to take military action against the Bosnian Serbs to -- unless they were to moderate their behaviour against Sarajevo. General Mladic's -- I'm reporting here his statement to me that if there was some form of foreign military intervention, he would attend to level the city of Sarajevo by intense artillery fire, and he had demonstrated for ten days or so before this meeting that he was quite capable of mounting quite a ferocious level of artillery fire against the city and therefore his threat was quite believable, and hence I reported this threat to my superior in headquarters UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would just like to direct your attention to a correction, if I may, Your Honour and General Wilson. It appears on line 17, the first part of your answer where it says: "This was a meeting that we had with General Plavsic."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Sorry, General Mladic and Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you sit down, line 17 of which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Line 17 of page 34 says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 17 of page 34 says -- can you explain the context of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have 34 -- Your Honour, I have -- my LiveNote is rapidly disappearing, line 34, the answer to the question appears at 15 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Line 17 of page 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you not able to stop it so that it does not disappear? I can see it at line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can see it at line 19 on this. I can't see as well as I used to be able to, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We're virtually two minutes from the break, so we'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have been involved in a military career for the greater share of your life, have you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Just a little over 34 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I won't ask you how old you are; it's none of my business. But a fair period of time. And I take it that you, in the work that you've done and the tours of duty that you have experienced, you've seen a fair amount of different conditions of war. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's true, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And one of the things that's kind of unique about the situation in Sarajevo was that for perhaps the first time in modern history - and I'm excludeing here, of course, Stalingrad - a battle was being fought in a city that was comprised of competing factions and civilians and the battle itself was in the city proper, which is kind of a unique situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't think it was unique. I was involved in the Battle of Beirut in very similar circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Since you've mentioned the Battle of Beirut, one of the things that is unique about warfare that occurs within an urban environment is that the rules of engagement become much more difficult to keep a bright line on. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so. The rules of engagement are quite clear. It's the interpretation of them that's perhaps a little more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not a military man, and I'm sure you can help me in that regard. And with regard to the issue of interpretation of the rules of engagement and now with regard specifically to Sarajevo, one of the realities was that in the city proper there were barracks that at one point were manned by JNA members; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was, as a matter of fact, if I'm not mistaken, the Marshal Tito barracks were barracks where supplies of both water and electricity had been cut off by the, as I think you called them, the Presidency forces on a number of occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware they had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your opinion, would that be a legitimate military act, to cut off the electricity or water in a region of town where there are military people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Are you talking there about cutting off electricity/water to the barracks or to the city?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm talking about cutting off water and electricity to an area of the city where there are barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the reason that's why I asked you previously the question about the rules of engagement, because that's why I think we're immediately find ourselves in an issue of interpretation, or maybe we don't, but that's what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: So if the aim, if you can limit it entirely to the barracks, that would be your aim. If it was impossible to only limit it to the barracks and you had to include part of the city, that would probably be a legitimate action.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And those are the kinds of discretionary decisions that have to be made by whoever is a commander during the period of time that they are engaged in that particular action.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not only by commanders, by individual soldiers too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to just fast-forward for a moment. Are you aware of the fact that NATO bombed Belgrade and in doing so bombed a transformer and radio stations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that. I'm aware that NATO bombed targets in Serbia. I was no longer engaged in the UN at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Would, in your opinion as a man with some substantial military experience, would the bombing of a radio station or a television station be a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It could be, provided you minimised collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And by the same token, would the bombing of or the destruction of the transformer that supplied electricity to your enemy, in an urban environment where there are civilians admittedly, would that be a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's a grey area, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Well, much of war is grey, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that when you arrived in Sarajevo the battle that you saw was, I think, what would be characterized, and I don't know if it was the parlance that was being used then but I know it's the parlance being used now, of asymmetric war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the precise definition of that. It's an American term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I happen to be American so that's probably the reason I'm using it. And what I'm referring to here, and perhaps you have a more precise term or a term that could help the Chamber in a way that I can't, is that you have disparate munitions or artillery or ammunition between the opposing forces, and you have disparate manpower. Those are the -- that's what I'm putting into the formula. I don't know whether that's sufficient or not.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: If you're saying that there's a gross discrepancy between the ability and the capabilities of both sides, is that your definition?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, if that's your definition, then I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Is that what you found when you came to Sarajevo, that there was a gross disparity between the two sides? And by that I mean between the ability and capabilities of the two sides.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: To be pedantic, when I first came to Sarajevo there was no fighting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: But as the situation developed, yes, it's true, there did appear to be a great weight in favour of the Bosnian Serb military forces as opposed to what I'd describe as the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the issue of the Presidency forces, you had -- you had made yourself aware, I would take it, before you came to Sarajevo of the nature and extent, to the best obviously that you could, of the Presidency forces, how many there were, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. When UNPROFOR deployed to Sarajevo in March of 1992, the operational focus of UNPROFOR was in Croatia, with the exception of my military observers who had an operational focus around Mostar and Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: What was happening in Sarajevo was simply the location to which the headquarters was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: What the military forces were, there was absolutely no interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There came a point in time when they became of some importance to you, did there not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When would that have been?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It happened on the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And on the 14th of May, when the conflict broke out, at that point in time did you educate yourself as to the number of forces that existed with the Bosnian Presidency, to the best that you could, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Sure. That began my education, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you give the Chamber an indication of what the strength was of those forces. And I'm not at this point talking about artillery or munitions because obviously I think it's well understood by all that there was a discrepancy or a disproportionate, shall we say, possession of those, but in terms of manpower.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Sure. When the war broke out on the 14th of May, the Presidency forces described their fighting elements as police forces. They made no particular claim to an army. It was only in the period perhaps a couple weeks later that I was able to meet somebody who described himself as commander of the army and a defence minister, in fact. But on the 14th of May, the forces that were fighting on behalf of the Presidency were police forces, armed with small arms. I actually met some of these fighters in the building -- my accommodation building where I was residing in in Dobrinja, Nedzarici. I only caught glimpses of the forces on the Serbian side. I certainly saw their way to fire. I saw fleeting views of their infantry during assaults around the area of what was known as the Rainbow Hotel. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We're getting closer.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After a couple of weeks, since you've given us a start date of the 14th, after a couple of weeks - and for purposes of my question, I'm not trying to tie you down to a particular date at all; I'm just trying to get a rough sense of time - after a couple of weeks, did you make at that point a determination, after you'd had an opportunity to meet with these gentlemen, what the size of the forces were of the Bosnian Presidency, after they transformed themselves what I understand to be, what they previously called themselves as police forces into an army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Sure. To my knowledge they made no claim to a particular number, but given the size of the city that they were defending, and they were defending it against infantry probes, they must have had some, I estimate, tens of thousands of people on the confrontation lines. If you want an educated guess, it would be in the order of 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to those 30.000 as an educated guess, and I understand it's that, and I'm not -- once again I'm not trying to tie you down to anything, but with regard to those 30.000 forces, were those forces deployed throughout the city? Were they in specific areas? Could you tell us what you learned in that regard? Once again, I'm talking at that initial time, a couple weeks after May 14th.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: If I could correct my previously educated guess, I would say perhaps 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe they were deployed on the confrontation line, and not in depth, if you understand the military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do. But could you define it for the Chamber and more importantly for the record so that we all have the same understanding.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: A military force is deployed in attack and defence normally in echelons, in lines, if you wish, so that it adds depth in defence, in particular, that an attacking force has to get through. It's both depth in manpower and depth in fire-support, in fire-power.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, we now find ourselves, if my calculations are correct, we now find ourselves in June; correct? Starting May 14th, we're now at the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: If you wish to nominate that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I wish to be accurate, and that's what I'm trying to get to, is an accuracy here with you with regard to certain things. At that point in time were you involved in negotiations by then with the various parties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Those negotiations started in perhaps the third week of May and continued through until about the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What knowledge did you have in the third week of May with regard to the status of Mr. Karadzic vis-a-vis who he represented and what importance he was to your negotiations, if any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was learning about the political situation in the third week of May. Dr. Karadzic, my understanding, was the President of the Bosnian Serb republic and presented himself as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to General Mladic, by the third week of May, what had you learned with regard to the status of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That was somewhat more debatable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I had known General Mladic since January of 1992 when he was the JNA commander in Knin. And when he arrived in Sarajevo sometime in the middle of May, I believe, he claimed then to be the commander of the emerging VRS; however, the JNA commanders that we were -- the JNA representatives in the negotiations over the evacuation of the barracks did on a number of occasions indicate that Mladic was a loose cannon. He was carrying out individual irresponsible actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, not only was he carrying out, as you've just put it, independent irresponsible actions, he was acting also, to use your language in your testimony - and I refer counsel to page 13068 of the prior testimony - that he was "out of control and acting independently and irrationally." Now, you've told us that one of the things that you did in your assessment of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I just ask that counsel, when you refer to a page, if you can give me a line site.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. Lines 17 through 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the things that you've mentioned to us here today is that your determination about the relationship of people was predicated in part on their demeanor, and I'd like to talk to you for a moment with regard to the -- your assessment of the demeanor of General Mladic. Having heard from representatives of the JNA that he was acting in such a fashion, being out of control, did you try to make an independent assessment for your purposes with regard to the accuracy of such a concern that was being voiced by those representatives?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Can I answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: On a number of occasions in late May and early June I -- with this discussion I'd had with the JNA representatives in mind, I had said to General Mladic that it was understood that he wasn't responsive to political direction or anybody else's direction. He was a lone maverick and he made it quite clear on a number of occasions that he was responsible to and responsive to the political leadership of the Bosnian Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that he was "responsible to and responsive to the political leadership of the Bosnian Serb people," you would be referring to his Commander-in-Chief, that would be Dr. Karadzic, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know that he was the Commander-in-Chief, but he was certainly his political boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was his superior.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he, General Mladic, was subordinate to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Mladic said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as a matter of fact, not only did he say that but you, in terms of your observations of the negotiations that occurred, saw that, and by that I mean you have pointed out to us that there were essentially differing views about the negotiation of what I'll call the freedom of the airport.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the views, that being the view of the JNA representative, that would have been General Panic and others, is -- I'm sorry, not "is" but "was," that they were willing to give up everything; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They were certainly flexible about what they were prepared to offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to use your language in your previous testimony at page 13059, lines 11 through 18, you said: "The JNA position was to effect the immediate evacuation of their forces at any cost as quickly as possible." And the evacuation of their forces and the airport negotiations, as a matter of fact, were all tied up with one another, were they not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I saw them as separate issues. And, in fact, Mladic said he wouldn't negotiate on the airport arrangement until the barracks had been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what Mladic said.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Well, then, let's talk about the barracks negotiation for a moment here. With regard to the Presidency position, that would be the Bosnian Presidency position, and their position was to bargain for the release of these forces to obtain arms and ammunition and concessions for humanitarian activity within the city.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say that the release of these forces -- that the bargaining there was for, among other things, to obtain arms and ammunition, what did they want? What did the Bosnian Presidency want in terms of arms and ammunition in terms of this negotiation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Okay. The detail of the negotiations was conducted by one of my officers, a Colonel Hoglund, so he was in the meetings for the many hours that they progressed. I was called in at critical times, so I'm not aware of the detail, bids and counter-bids, that took place. I am aware that in the end that two, I recall, but I read somewhere else that three semi-trailer loads of small-arms weapons were handed over to the Presidency forces as a result of the deal that was struck between General Panic and the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to -- with regard to the Bosnian Presidency forces' negotiations, considering what your mandate was, irrespective of the type of munitions that were being negotiated for, I take it that what the Presidency was negotiating for was more weapons, not less.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They wanted more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that was for the purpose of continuing - and I'm asking the question if you took this into your calculations when you were trying to close these negotiations - that was for the purpose of continuing the war efforts. They didn't ask for more weapons just on a whim; they wanted more weapons so they could be armed for purposes of making themselves stronger with regard to what was going on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know what their purpose was, but it would be a reasonable assumption that they wanted to continue the fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Counsel, when you say "more weapons," you're saying they wanted more weapons than the Bosnian Serbs had, or did they want more weapons than they would have been offered, if there was any offer at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I -- thank you. Clearly, not a very clear question and I will clear -- clean it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In following the Judge's question, the -- without getting into the details, because that, I understand, you were not privy to. What the Bosnian Presidency wanted was more weapons than they had at the time for their forces.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously, they would have liked more weapons than the Serbian forces had, but that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. There were various ambit bids. They wanted a greater number than they got in the end, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that in and of itself is not an uncommon thing to occur during these negotiations processes; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. That's normal in that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because, after all, as we all know, war is not illegal. Nations can fight against each other. There's nothing wrong with that; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be pedantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be moving in the wrong way, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not moving in the wrong way. When you say "what the Bosnian Presidency wanted was more weapons than they had at the time for their forces," what do we mean? Do we mean they had maybe 10 tanks, and they wanted 11 or 20, or do we mean they wanted to amend what they had, even if it was only by one, so what they had before is more than -- is less than what they now have by one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not, by virtue of your position in terms of the negotiations, you have that particular kind of information with regard to the various ambits that the Bosnian Presidency were seeking to achieve, and if you can be of some help to us in that regard, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I think as an illustration one -- if one proposed that the Presidency forces may have had 15.000 small-arms weapons before the negotiations commenced, the negotiating process was to acquire an additional, say, 5.000 weapons, so at the end of the process they would have 15.000 weapons. That's what the negotiation was about. They would end up with more weapons at the end of it than they had before they commenced the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are we good?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the Bosnian Serb position, which was being at that time championed by Mladic, if I'm not mistaken, was not to hand over any weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Which was in direct contradiction with the JNA position.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the evacuation of the barracks, the barracks were ultimately evacuated somewhat successfully, and by that I mean young JNA soldiers left the barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to Marshal Tito barracks, during the time that they were evacuated from those barracks, I take it that the agreement between the parties, and the parties then being, if I'm understanding correctly, the Bosnian Presidency, General Panic on behalf of his young soldiers, and General Mladic on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs, was that these forces would be evacuated and during that period of time there would be no attack upon them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That was the agreement and that's what, in fact, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the evacuation of those barracks, the Marshal Tito barracks, no injuries or casualties were suffered.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there were also other barracks that were being evacuated at the same time. When I say "same time," I don't mean precisely the same time, but around that period of time, where there were other JNA soldiers, and is your answer the same with regard to them? That they, too, suffered no casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. On the fourth barracks to be evacuated, in the last -- within the urban area of Sarajevo, there were, I believe, 30 soldiers who went missing actually during the process of leaving the barracks and arriving outside the city. Now, what exactly happened to those people is unclear. They ran up against a position, and there was some firing that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They may have been killed. They may have been taken prisoner. They may have deserted. But there was some 30 missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: If I can finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: One might attribute that this operation was less than successful was because of a poorly planned and executed evacuation. They began this evacuation at twilight. With quite a large convoy and without warning anybody along the route they were coming, it was almost inevitable something like this would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that "it was almost inevitable something like this would happen," I take it, then, what you mean by that that the forces of the Bosnian Presidency in such a situation, seeing such a convoy, would find it necessary to fire upon them, for some reasons, none of which we know about.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know if it was Presidency forces that fired on them. It could have been Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, really?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It happened in the dark, and there was mass confusion. I don't think anyone can accuse the Presidency forces of that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So in your mind, once this occurred, did this create any difficulties with regard to the negotiation process that you were in for further negotiations, once these young men had been fired upon by whomever they had been fired upon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: To be honest, the parties seemed to shrug their shoulders and accept that it was an incident, and they moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: But I certainly learned a very strong lesson from it, that we should insist upon a properly planned operation before we became involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the next negotiation, and if I'm chronologically accurate, during that period of time you were engaged in shuttle diplomacy because, in fact, the Bosnian Presidency refused to negotiate with their certain Serb counter-parts; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And were those Bosnian Serbs that they refused to negotiate with or were those members of the JNA that they were refusing to negotiate with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They were refusing to meet the political leadership of the Bosnian Serb organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. That was something that was communicated, was it not, to the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and it was an arrangement that continued on through to my time in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to their refusal to negotiate with the Bosnian Serb leadership, did that, in your mind, constitute difficulties concerning their stated purpose to retain a fully integrated ethnically inter-twined Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know I'm competent to answer that. I mean, it made negotiating logistically more difficult, but I've got no idea what the political impact was. That's not my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well you, as a matter of fact, took the position, did you not, that the Bosnian Presidency stated political position was to retain a fully integrated ethnically intertwined Bosnia-Herzegovina? That was clear in 1992 and subsequently all through 1993. You've testified to that, and I refer the Court and counsel to page 13052, lines 9 through 13.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm repeating statements made to me on numerous occasions by the Bosnian Serb leadership in making that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. You personally experienced, however, the reality of the situation, which is that one group refused to meet with the other group.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. It makes it a little difficult to come to an accord, doesn't it, if one group refuses to meet with the other group?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, physically refused to meet with them but certainly were prepared to consider the negotiating position of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm trying to understand something, which is with regard to the airport negotiation, is it your testimony that in that regard, the demeanor that you saw between the participants was such that you determined during the negotiation for the airport that Mladic was subordinate to Panic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That was the opinion I formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the difficulty that was occurring at that time was that Mladic was refusing to hand over the airport; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That was his negotiating position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall that Karadzic took Mladic into a room because of his incalcitrance, and you could hear Karadzic screaming at Mladic, and after the screaming session was over, Karadzic came out and said there will be no further problems. And I'm, essentially I'm paraphrasing what I understood your testimony to be, but I'm trying to get to, rather than your testimony, the reality of what occurred.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Once again, to be pedantic, I don't know the reason for Karadzic taking Mladic into the other room, but yes, there was a violent disagreement which you could hear through the walls of the room we were in, and when they returned to the negotiations, it's true that Karadzic's position prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In that regard, Karadzic's position at that time was the precise position of Panic, which is, Let's get the airport negotiated and taken care of, and both of them were in disagreement with General Mladic, the individual who at least one party, and by that I mean Panic, had indicated some concern about, let's say, his control issues and clearly you had seen or heard -- you didn't see it, you heard that there was some need to use a fair measure of force upon the man in order to bring him to the table.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Panic -- General Panic, head of the JNA, was not involved in the airport negotiations at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The military representative there was General Mladic, and I at the time understood his authority extended over the JNA forces which remained in the Sarajevo area and would have been, in my view, present at the airport. Panic, as I recall, was only interested in the evacuation of the barracks. The last of them was -- wrong. He was only interested in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in your conversations with General Mladic, General Mladic made it very clear to you, and I think it was probably something that was of importance to you in trying to determine who the players -- not only who the players were but what their lines of authority were. He made it very clear to you that he was subordinate to the political leadership of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Both through his statements on a number of occasions and also by his demeanor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the time that you were in Sarajevo, did you have working for you in UNPROFOR a British officer named Pyres Tucker? Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The name doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive information from any UNPROFOR Canadian officers concerning indications that it was common knowledge through investigations carried out by the United Nations that Muslim forces did on occasion shell their own civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I can't remember such a conversation. I can remember a report that was associated with the bread line attack. It was a crater analysis of where the mortars had landed which could not rule out the possibility that there were potential mortar positions along the line of attack so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was an investigation that was carried out by the French; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The French, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was an investigation that you discussed in your statement, I believe at paragraph 51 of the statement that you were discussing with Mr. Harmon earlier today, that the French had done the investigation and they couldn't come up with a conclusive determination as to who had done that particular shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Did you receive information -- first of all, do you know of a gentleman by the name of Richard Mole, or Mole? I could be pronouncing it incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: A general? I think so. I think I know a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, he may be a general now.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can talk about him, and I might recall him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was a senior UNMO from September to December.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Somebody you had contact with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from him that there were potential incidents that occurred where the Presidency forces may well have been, I don't want to say "targeting," but I'll say attacking their own areas so they could assist in the view that the population of Sarajevo was beleaguered and that they may well have fired upon their own city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't recall such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of -- it may have been after your time there, are you aware of any of the opinions of, I believe, his name is Michael Rose with regard -- once again, this same issue, of whether or not some of these forces were, in fact -- and by that I mean the Bosnian Presidency forces were, in fact -- that there had been information that they were at some point firing on their own areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was well gone by the time Michael Rose appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might be of some assistance to my colleague, that's information taken from the Galic trial judgement at paragraph 211.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Sarajevo, were you aware of the fact that there was a tunnel that was in the control of the Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Not while I was in Sarajevo but subsequently, yes, I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not that tunnel was a tunnel that the Presidency forces allowed the civilian population to depart from or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know who went through the tunnel, but I do know that the political leaders of the Presidency were able to move about when the city was invested, so I presume that they may have had the opportunity to use that tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive information in your capacity as an observer that that tunnel was being used for purposes of bringing any weapons or other aid and materials to the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm unaware of the detail of what went through the tunnel, but I think it's reasonable to assume that some sort of assistance for their military action would have gone through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive any kind of information -- what I should say, really, similar information with regard to the use of the airport for bringing in material supplies to the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I would think that's highly unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: A system was set up which allowed the Serbs to actually supervise the detail of the cargo outside the country where it was led. It's highly unlikely that any sort of contraband like that would make it through the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to September of 1992, you were at that point involved, I believe, in another negotiation, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, the evacuation of the JNA from the area surrounding Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And just briefly with regard to that particular negotiation, am I accurate in stating that in October 1992, the JNA unilaterally executed a well-conducted withdrawal broadly in accordance with the agreement that you had negotiated, and the Croatians, on the other hand, failed to adhere to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I don't see any relevance to the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. To the extent this is a prefatory question to my next question which deals with whether or not this gentleman obtained information concerning the Bosnian Presidency forces and the Croatian forces combining together for purposes of conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How is this question that you intend to ask predicated on the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if there has been a -- if there has been a violation by one of the parties to a negotiated disagreement and that party then, here the Croatians, then begin to work with the Bosnian Presidency for purposes of resisting their perceived enemy at the time and that information is communicated to the other side or they become aware of it, it certainly impacts on ultimate issues concerning how one views intent and notice and the reaction of the Serbian -- and by that I'm not referring to the Bosnian Serbs but the Serbian political structure in future days. And it really deals directly with some of the issues that were raised by Mr. Harmon in his opening statement with regard to forecasting in 1992 a series of events that ultimately, as I understand his theory of prosecution, are, shall we say, that gestate through that period of time and are given birth at the point in time that our client becomes the Chief of Staff of the VJ. But if that seems a too long a road to take, and in looking at you, I have that sneaking suspicion it may well be, I'm willing to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome to interpret my body language.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Maybe I've gotten wrapped up in General Wilson in that. I have one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That the Croatians, however, failed to adhere to the guidelines of the agreement and subsequently invaded Serb-held territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina with elements of their regular army. Now, first of all, I understand that was your particular view of what occurred in terms of the negotiation that you had put together; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, but there was never an agreement between the two parties on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Did you -- did you have discussions with any members of the Bosnian Serbs concerning this particular subsequent invasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, only General Bobetko, General Bobetko of the Croatian forces, and a JNA general whom I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "a JNA general," was that somebody you had been actively involved in in terms of these negotiation processes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We had a couple of hours' discussion during this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it -- and I understand you don't remember his name, but I take it that he was somewhat exercised by the fact that he had engaged in -- not he, but the JNA had engaged in a unilateral withdrawal and then an area that they had withdrawn from was invaded. He was not particular pleased about it, was he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I never saw him after he had executed the withdrawal. But I have to say that he acted in the most professional manner. He took note of what their proposal was but indicated that he would not sign any bit of paper. It would then be a point of honour to him that he didn't want to be associated with the withdrawal of the JNA from territory. But when the withdrawal was executed some days later, it was done in a very professional operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the parties that you're dealing with, and I understand that the withdrawal was done professionally, and I take it by that there was no fire and no -- there were no casualties in terms of the withdrawal. Were these discussions that you had in terms of the success of these kinds of withdrawals, were these discussions that you had with Dr. Karadzic in terms of after the withdrawal was successful?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. At that time I had no negotiation -- I had no role in negotiating with the Bosnian Serb political leadership at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was a subordinate officer working out of UNPROFOR headquarters. Those negotiations from the end of June no longer involved me and would have been carried out, more than likely, by Mr. Thornberry, the senior political officer, and perhaps General Morillon or General Mackenzie.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So your duties passed into another area then, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I was used as a -- you might call it a project negotiator. When something came up that there was nobody else obvious to do it, then I was invited to do that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sounds like you were used as a closer on a fair number of different occasions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I had been there a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned to us in your direct testimony that when asked, Slobodan Milosevic indicated in one-to-one conversations that he had limited influence on the other parties, and I take it by that specifically the influence would be upon Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic, when he said he had limited influence.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
