utterances.text: He did make that statement from time to time. He had a variety of responses, and that was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the other one that he -- that he mentioned, as I understand it, was that he had no authority over these individuals.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, he never at any point claimed any authority. The question was the degree of influence that he may or may not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you're talking influence, influence is a relatively, and I'm sure it's something that you were quite familiar with, is a relatively popular tool in the world of diplomacy and negotiation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it's a very broad term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed so. Indeed so. And with regard to that term, the term of "influence," it takes into account such issues as political favors, economic issues.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It could also include the turning off of any aid or support that might be provided, both in material or political, or diplomatic sense also.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It could be the imposition of an embargo or the lifting of an embargo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: A water type one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you saw, you experienced both of the use of this kind of influence by the international community with regard to the general situation. By that I mean the embargoes, whether they were successful or not being an entirely different matter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They may have been limited influence, a great deal of influence, but nevertheless you would not say that in that situation, when those particular kinds of events were occurring, by that I mean international embargoes, that that would be a matter of control now, would you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Certainly one of influence. I'm not sure what you're implying by "control." I mean, the embargo attempts to influence, if you wish, or to push the authorities in the former Yugoslavia in a certain direction. It can't physically make them do it. There's not a gun at the head. It's a strong suggestion that this would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the threat of bombing, which also was something that was discussed on a number of different occasions, but during your tenure in Sarajevo, that was another example of what we call influence, which is, Listen, if you don't come up to the table and start doing what we believe is appropriate - and once again, I'm not putting value judgements on any of these things - there is this option that you may be bombed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a threat.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, that particular threat was a threat, as I recall it, that was the same threat that Mladic engaged in in the paragraph that you were so kind to discuss with Mr. Harmon, in which he says, if I understand, basically, If you bomb us, then we're going to -- or I'm going to shell Sarajevo. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic is very believable. I mean, he had -- his very recent actions in the two weeks before that made such a threat very believable. Another characteristic of General Mladic was generally what he said he'd do, he did it. Whether he liked the consequences is another matter, but he was a man of his word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. And in the context of the negotiations that you were going through and that you were privy to, one of the things that you always had to gauge was exactly what you just mentioned, which is when the party says something, are they going to follow through?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's something that is being done by all of the parties with regard to these negotiations, whether they be in peace, but more specifically when these negotiations are occurring in a war setting.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: And I might say that General Mladic, with 200 pieces of artillery surrounding a city, is a more credible threat than a rather vague threat done through the international media that air attacks might under certain circumstances be launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that was a threat that just took a long time for NATO to get to the point of when they made the determination to do that. But when they decided to pull the trigger, they pulled the trigger.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: But at the time that paragraph was drafted, Mladic was more incredible than the international air threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your estimation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In my estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did others share your view in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know what I was told. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the information with regard to international bombing of that region, whether the information was communicated throughout Bosnia and in Belgrade? Did you tell, for example, Milosevic this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. I had no contact with Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether others discussed this with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you involved in any discussions where the issue of how Milosevic would respond to the notion that NATO or the international community was going to bomb Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was certainly aware and received cable traffic that there was support from the -- from President Milosevic in regard to opening the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He didn't want to get bombed, did he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't know why he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One final question, which is surrounding Sarajevo there are a number of high points; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And one of them is, I believe, an area called Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, although I'm unaware of its exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your tenure in Sarajevo was Mount Igman under the control of the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mount Igman came to my attention in 1993 during the negotiations in the Geneva, and my understanding was that the Presidency forces had carried out some military operation which resulted in the capture of that feature. There had been a counter-attack, a successful counter-attack, by the Bosnian Serb forces who had cleared the Presidency of that position, and that to allow the negotiations to proceed, a UN force was placed on the mountain and the opposing forces, the Presidency and the Serb forces, withdrew from that area. It was a sort of demilitarization process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, what do you mean, at page 66, line 12, by "cleared the Presidency" of that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I don't have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, page 66 on your screen. On your screen, line 12, you said: "There had been a counter-attack, a successful counter-attack, by the Bosnian Serb forces who had cleared the Presidency of that position."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant to say there, Your Honour, the Presidency military forces. The Bosnian Serb military forces through a counter-attack had driven the Presidency military forces, the Muslim forces, away from the objective that they had recently captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to your recollection, was Mount Igman then turned over to UNPROFOR forces by Serbian forces or by the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I understand by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harmon, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a question just on one point, General Wilson. My colleague referred to a portion of your previous testimony Exhibit 142, the transcript of you previous evidence on the 17th of May, 2005, in which part of your answer reads as follows: "I raised those issues." "Was there some concern from the JNA representatives at the barracks negotiation that Mladic was out of control and acting independently and irrationally?" So my question is there was some concern of JNA representatives. Which representatives expressed that concern?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That would have been General Boskovic, who was at that stage leading the negotiations, and also Colonel Kardelj, I think his name was. He was the JNA liaison officer to UNPROFOR and was participating also in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So at page 54 of the transcript, when my colleague asked you: "Did General Panic express concern about control issues over Mladic," and you essentially said yes, do you wish to clarify that answer that you gave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Then I've given an incorrect answer. The only disagreement that I recall between General Panic and General Mladic was over the issue of weapons in terms of the barracks negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so to clarify the question and answer, General Panic was not one of those individuals from the JNA who expressed concern about control issues over Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. And to my knowledge, General Panic did not talk to General Mladic about his conduct of, say, artillery attacks on the city, and if he had, I wouldn't have understood it because I don't speak the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question. Did you testify in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, thank you very much for coming to testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down. And travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland will lead the next witness, who is an expert witness, Patrick Treanor, Your Honour. If we can have a few minutes to readjust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: My name is Patrick Joseph Treanor. I was born on 14 February 1947.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before I deal briefly with your academic qualifications and your relevant work experience, I just want to remind you that as we both speak the same language, we need to remember to pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you received a Bachelor of Arts degree in modern languages from the College of the Holy Cross in Massachusetts, USA, in 1968; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You received a Masters degree in Russian and Eastern European studies in 1970 from the Yale University Graduate School in Connecticut, in the United States?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You received a Doctor of Philosophy from the University of London in the United Kingdom in 1999 after completing a course of study at the School of Slavonic and East European Studies in Bulgarian history.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And having said that, receiving the doctorate, you would prefer in these proceedings to be referred to as Mr. Treanor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You began your professional career as an intelligence analyst in the Federal Research Division of the US Library of Congress in 1977 until 1980, and that work involved analysis of Yugoslav military and related affairs; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In late 1980 you began work as a historian and later senior historian in the Office of Special Investigations of the US Department of Justice, until 1994.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During that time you assisted in the investigation and litigation of cases of alleged Nazi war criminals living in the USA, and your responsibility centered on the identification, research, and analysis of wartime and post-war documentation, including Yugoslav documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The work involved planning and carrying out independent investigative research at archives in several countries in North America, Europe, and the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From July 1994 to the present, you've been engaged first as a research officer for the Office of the Prosecutor and subsequently as Head of the Legal Research Team and Senior Research Officer, a post you assumed in February 1998?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: The name of the team is the Leadership Research Team. Yes, I became the head of that team in 1998. I became the acting head at the end of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in that position you conducted your own research and supervised the research efforts of others on your team?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That work primarily involved the collection and analysis of original documentary and published materials relating to the organisation and activities of the various parties involved in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and more specifically to the Serb and Bosnian Serb governmental organs and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the purposes of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The materials included the records of governments, political parties, and military units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've been somewhat patient, obviously, because I understand the intent to get some information out of the way, but I think at this point, it may be of some importance for the witness to testify as opposed to answer yes-or-no questions, as regards to what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what materials did you review -- have you reviewed over the last 14 years?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, over the last 14 years, I've been involved in the collection of documents in the region of the former Yugoslavia, which involves reviewing documents in situ. I've also reviewed documents that were collected by other OTP staff, either in the region itself or via request for assistance from authorities in the region. The types of documents that I've reviewed fall into several categories. I'll just name them. One category would be what we call open sources, that is, newspapers and magazines from the region of the former Yugoslavia. We have made a systematic effort over the years to collect as many newspapers and magazines published in the region during the periods of the conflict and the years before and indeed after. We now have a collection of some 31.000 separate issues of newspapers and magazines. We also made -- we have also made an effort to collect the Official Gazettes of the various entities in the former Yugoslavia. I think we have complete -- or at least almost complete sets of the Official Gazettes of all the entities in the former Yugoslavia for the period of the conflicts there, and by "the conflicts," I mean the period from, say, 1991 to 1995, as well as for some periods -- years before those dates and after those dates. Our original documentation includes records of political parties, records of governments, and military records. The type of records that I particularly work with would include documents such as minutes of meetings, transcripts of meetings, orders, decisions, correspondence. I've also reviewed numerous, if I can use the term, "intercepted communications" between members of various parties to the conflicts there. Those would be conversations that were intercepted by another party to the conflict and have been made available to OTP in various fashions. I think that about covers it, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As team leader of the LRT, is it common practice to supervise the production of reports for investigations and trial teams?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. A part of my duties is to -- certainly to assist my staff in doing their research, guiding them to appropriate collections of documents, for instance, and to review their work product, as well as to prepare my own analyses, which would also include incorporating analyses which had been made by other members of the team into a joint -- into a joint product.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at a quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what's your proficiency in the language that's commonly referred to as Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I have a very good reading knowledge of the language. I can conduct rudimentary conversation, certainly, and understand it fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified before this Tribunal previously, once in the Brdjanin case in July and October 2003 and then in the Krajisnik case in February 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I believe those dates are correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In preparation for and in support of that testimony, did you prepare some reports that were subsequently tendered into evidence in those cases?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. I think there was one report for the Brdjanin case and another report for the Krajisnik case. Each of those reports was submitted under my name; however, other individuals worked in the preparation as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you prepared for this case, did you not, the report entitled "the Belgrade leadership and the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia 1990 to 1995," which is dated the 1st of September, 2008?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's the latest version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That report describes several aspects in the breakup of the SFRY in the years 1990 to 1995, and it concerns in particular the goals of the Serbian leaders during this process and the state structures they sought to create for the Serbian people in pursuit of those goals; does it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object as leading. It also calls for a series of conclusions which the report may or may not actually define, and I would ask once again that the gentleman answer questions and develop his testimony as apart to having the Prosecution testify and having him answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that sentence was contained in the in the introduction to the report, and I was clearly just summarising what the report was about before we got into particular questions about the aim of the report to which Mr. Treanor would be answering the questions to. So that was my last question on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but may you put questions, please, to Mr. Treanor, and let him answer and testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would the Registry please call up 00646.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said 066 or 006?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I understood the number to be 06646.01, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, do you recognize that this is the report that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the aim of the report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, in the report I describe within the context of the dissolution of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which I'll refer to as the SFRY, the goals that were adopted by the Serbian leadership within that process. The Serbian leadership is a group which I define as those persons holding the highest level, civilian and military positions within Serbia; the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the FRY; the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the RSK; and Republika Srpska, the RS. I describe in particular the developments of those entities, again within the context of the dissolution of the former SFRY with the focus on the goals that those leaders had set for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you provide the Court with some understanding of the nature of the documents that are cited in that report and upon which you relied, further issues you focused on and the conclusions you drew?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. The types of documents I use in the report are the type that I described at the beginning of my testimony as the type of documents I generally work with. They are official documents of the various Serbian entities, documents such as minutes and transcripts of meetings, laws, decisions, constitutions. There are also some press items that are used. Those are -- typically are the, say, speeches of leaders that were given on particular occasions and published in the press. I also use some UN documents, such as UN Security Council resolutions, presidential statements, and -- I think those are the main categories of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What methodology did you use in the criteria, what criteria were chosen by you in reviewing and selecting these documents?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, let me answer that question by saying that -- going back to the fact that I've been engaged in collecting and reviewing documents from the former Yugoslavia for almost 15 years -- over 14 years. In the course of that process, I have personally made an effort, and others in OTP have made an effort, to systematically collect various categories of documents. I mentioned earlier the open sources of the press, for instance, Official Gazettes. But more importantly, I think, for this case we have categories of documents, such as the records of various types of meetings. So I've made it my business to collect and review, for instance, all the records of meetings of the Bosnian Serb Presidency, as the Presidency of Republika Srpska; all the records of meetings of the Bosnian Serb assembly; the records of meetings of the FRY's Supreme Defence Council, the SDC. So there are whole categories of documents which I have reviewed and made notes or summaries of, and that material is part of my tool bag, if you will. When I'm asked to produce a report, I go into my collection of summaries and notes on documents, most of which are embodied in a CaseMap format. Our team has its own CaseMap. I put many of the documents in there myself and other people put things there as well under my direction. So I have all that available to me when dealing with a specific request for a report. So that material is pre-existing, if you will. When I get a request for a report such as this one, I then go into that body of material and review items that I -- that I think -- review and select items that I think may be relevant to the subject, to the report. The report, of course -- writing a report of this nature takes place within the context of certain constraints, the most important being time and space. Ordinarily, the trial team wants it pretty fast and also wants to keep it short, concise, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. So within the -- within the framework of the type of material that I've been describing, which is based on a systematic review of various categories of documents from the region, I produced this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, in keeping with your order of the 27th of October, I will, at the completion of Mr. Treanor's testimony, be seeking to tender his CV, the report, and the documents that are cited in that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Sutherland, but I'm not quite sure that your question has been answered. Your question was specifically what methodology was being used and what criteria were used. We've been told, for instance, "that I think for this case we have categories of documents, such as the records of various types of meetings." Now, on what criteria do we choose some and not others, and how do we determine relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the categories of documents that I have reviewed include the records that we have available in OTP, and again they become available after efforts to obtain them for, for instance, the highest level policy-making bodies of the entities in the former Yugoslavia and some of the political parties. So in the case of this report, particularly important are the records of the Presidency of the SFRY, the records of the assembly of the Republika Srpska, the Official Gazettes of the FRY --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. You've told us that, sir. The question is: What criteria do you use to pick on certain types of records and not others? You said, as I said earlier, "for this case we have categories of documents such as the records of various types of meetings," and a little later you said you pick them on the basis of relevance. The question is: How do you determine relevance and how do you -- what criteria do you use to pick on certain documents and not others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me clarify that. I have, as I say, available to me these various collections of records, and I select from those various collections those portions of individual records which, in my judgement, are relevant to the topic in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On what criteria is your judgement based, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my judgement is based on my knowledge of the subjects and my -- my personal judgement as to whether a particular item is relevant to the topic that I was requested to produce a report on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but, you see, you're testifying as an expert. As an expert we expect that you have certain expertise, certain principles within your area of expertise that guide you in making your selection. I'm trying to find out what those are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well, I'm a historian by profession, and we don't use a -- some sort of numerical or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- analytical framework of that sort. It's based on the judgement of the individual researcher as to what is "relevant."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. That's the problem, sir, because then it may very well be that you left certain documents that are relevant and brought in documents that are not relevant if you don't have a system of doing things, and this is the problem. And if you say you don't use some sort of -- well, the sentence is incomplete. Then the question becomes: How do we take this report as an expert report? Because if you say you're a historian, anybody can write history, is that what you're saying, and pick up facts that he wants to pick up, based on his personal judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, training for a historian involves doing research and producing an analytical product, and extensive analytical product, usually referred to as a thesis or a dissertation on a particular topic, and that product of thesis or dissertation on a particular topic. And that product of thesis or dissertation is reviewed by usually senior people in the field, and they pass judgement on it. There is, as I said, there is no mathematical key to how you select documents. It's a judgemental question, and one develops one's judgement in this field by, A, reading history and, B, doing research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, are there any objective structures in the report constituted by the historical and factual data, and have you used a course of discretion in selecting certain facts from others? Because I imagine that there is no historical work without at least some hypothetical presumptions that later on are verified on the facts, which is to say that there is no history without some degree of subjectivity, but at the same time that history should not be purely arbitrarily impersonal. Is the subjectivity based on the selection of the most relevant facts in relation to some hypothetical lines of thinking that are expressed in the conclusions of the report? I don't know if I am confusing you or clarifying the situation, because I believe that in any historical report, there are always some degree of subjectivity, but it's not the subjectivity that is purely personal of the researcher but a subjectivity that consists of selecting certain paths of thinking according to the general overall perspective of the situation. Is that your case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you might have helped a bit, Your Honour. As a general matter, I would say that that is the case. As you've stated, there is always an element of subjectivity or even ideological approach that each person is imbued with when they approach particular material and seek to analyse it. Perhaps it would assist if I note -- if I noted the following: In tracing the developments of the various entities that I mentioned, I sought to do that - again, I sought to do that; perhaps I didn't succeed - in a uniform fashion by picking the same types of documents from each entity which chronicle their development from the beginning of some sort of declaration to the establishment of an autonomous area to the establishment of a republic. What does the constitution say about what the organs of that power will be? Who occupied the offices? Again, I attempted to do that for each of the entities that I was describing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: There is in paragraph 4 of the introduction: The focus, you said, is rather on the goals of the Serbian leaders and the extent to which they achieve them. The facts recorded thus do not by any means represent the whole history of the conflict of the region, but there will be essential elements in any such telling." So you have started already saying what are the objectives of the research, the goals of the research. This goal was given to you by the Prosecution or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: -- or were you free in the selection of the goals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Prosecution asked for a report on a -- of a particular nature, and that's what I've described in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So we must say that your research is not absolutely personally value-free because you have been given a task to comply with in the sense that you have been given a purpose and a task, some objectives. Now, the important point is that you have rendered, to the extent of your knowledge, with methodology, tools, and so on, the best product that you were able to achieve. Are you sure that this is the best you could -- that you could have achieved in producing the prescribed goals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the task was set by the trial team and within the framework of that task, I was free to do whatever I wanted to, basically. Could I have produced a better product? Given more time and more space, it would have been more complete and much longer. But I think that the main outlines of the topic are in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say the task was given by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, by the trial team. I'm sorry, I may have misspoken. The trial team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Trial team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to pick up something now that was said in answer to Judge David's questions. You say: "As you have stated, there is always an element of subjectivity or even ideological approach that each person is imbued with when they approach particular material and seek to analyse it." Were you driven by that in compiling your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that based on the theoretical literature on this topic with which I have some familiarity, although not a deep one, I'm told that, as Judge David was saying, that everyone sort of has some sort of bias or another, and then they may not realize it. I mean, I'm from the United States. It's a liberal democracy. We believe in equal rights in the United States and the equality of all its citizens, et cetera, et cetera, so that's the -- something that I suppose will affect my approach to anything, as opposed to somebody who, for instance, might have come from the former Soviet Union and believed in -- was a Marxist, et cetera, et cetera. So that type of bias operates subconsciously or unconsciously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand your reference to the United States and Russia. My question to you was: Were you driven by that subjectivity and ideological approach in compiling this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was trying to describe what my ideology is. That was my reference to the United States. That informs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how did you apply that ideology in the compilation of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated, I think that that type of thing is generally -- operates subconsciously or unconsciously. I couldn't say how I consciously applied it. Someone else who has a different -- from a different ideological background may have approached this in an entirely different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, in addition, just because of your answer, there is no question that every work of history or in the social sciences is surrounded by implicit ideological options, but one thing are the ideological options, and the second thing are the strict structure of an objective research. You have obtained a Ph.D. in a US university, or in any other university, and certainly your masters will have a structure, your research, in such a way that you will maximize the objective in parenthesis of the factual data and of the interpretation of the data in order to get it purer from obscure ideological connotations, implying that certainly values are there in any thinking. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And so you might have some options from what part of the world you come, but there is a universal set of rules concerning the minimal standards of a scientific objective piece. Are you following? Are you in agreement with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And my question is to you: Despite this ideological bending that anyone from various part of the world has, are you convinced that you have insisted upon the most extreme objectivity on factual -- on factual data and underlining interpretations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I believe that's true, and let me give an explanation to that directly related to the report. The report is based on certain documents, which I've mentioned, and the -- each paragraph is referenced to a particular document and generally each paragraph is a description or a summary or an extract from the contents of that document. I sought to make no -- draw no interpretive conclusions from any document or any set of those documents. In other words, just -- I sought to simply lay out in a string, if you will, usually chronologically in each section, what the contents of each document that would be important to consider in the context of this report, what that document says, again without drawing any conclusions of my own or putting any interpretation on them. Now, it's given, of course, that I selected the documents based on my judgement, and I selected the portions of the documents that I wanted to use, and I'm the one that is responsible for the -- for the summaries of the documents, but -- as opposed to a standard work of historical research where the historian will feel free, indeed feel compelled, to make various interpretations and judgements. I sought to refrain from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, for the purposes of your testimony, you also selected a number of documents to assist the Court in understanding your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I selected a number of documents that were not cited in the reports that I thought might also be useful. Again, when I wrote the report, there were certain constraints of time and space in producing it for the purposes of this testimony. Of course, we're not going to use nearly all the documents that are cited in the report, so I thought it might be beneficial to introduce some new ones which would shed additional light on some of the matters raised in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, Mr. Treanor has binders of documents in front of him which have the B/C/S versions of the documents, and I would seek Your Honours' leave that he be allowed to refer to those. I have shown them to my colleague Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, so he has reviewed those binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct. I have reviewed the binders. I do have a question, however, with regard to the issue of the interpretation and translation of that material. As I understand what we're about to do is that Mr. Treanor, who has some proficiency in reading the language, is, I take it, going to be commenting and translating, he's going to be performing the function of a translator and potentially an interpreter - and I make a distinction as between the two, for obvious reasons - with regard to source documents themselves which I think, quite frankly, poses a problem. Because if we do not have official interpretations of those documents, something which all parties can rely upon, and I don't know whether or not Mr. Treanor has had the opportunity to take the proficiency examination of an interpreter or translator, such that there is a common basis for his understanding of the language and the subtleties of the language specifically as it deals with matters before the Tribunal and any kind of legal issues that could occur, I believe that we may run into a rather unfortunate problem with regard to the issue of translation as well as interpretation with regard to the content of those documents upon which he relies, which he wishes to share with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor is going to give his opinion on the documents. The documents are going to come in e-court. There's a translation there, and there's also the B/C/S version. In order to assist him, he has the documents, the B/C/S version of the documents, in front of him so that he can go to those documents in order to give his opinion to whatever question I may put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say there's an official translation of the documents that you are going to show him here?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, the Rule 65 ter translations so there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I'm not bothered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To the extent -- to the extent that there may be -- we'll see how this progresses. There may be a distinction between what Mr. Treanor believes the document says and what the official translation presents could be an entirely different issue. But for the moment I think we'll be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based upon the specific methodology, and I'm pleased of hear of a methodology that we're going to be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can we begin then by discussing the documents you selected, and perhaps we can begin with the speech of the President of the Presidency of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, in the Republic of Serbian Assembly on the 26th of June, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if document number 06812 could be brought up onto the screen, please. In the B/C/S it's page number 1, and in the English translation it's on page number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, did you say 06813 or 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 06812, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Perhaps you could start, Mr. Treanor, by just putting briefly that speech into context.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This speech was given in June 1990, as has been mentioned. At that time the process of the dissolution of the SFRY was progressing to the extent that at the beginning of 1990, the ruling party of the SFRY, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, essentially dissolved. Yugoslavia had been a one-party state until that time. After the -- indeed, in some cases before the dissolution of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, non-communist parties were formed in the various republics of the SFRY, and those parties, and indeed some members of the League of Communists in the various republics, raised the demand for multi-party elections, which hitherto had not taken place in the SFRY. Such elections had taken place in Slovenia and Croatia in the spring of 1990, in April, and those elections resulted in the victory of non-communist parties in those republics; that is, non-communist parties elected the majority of members of the assemblies of those republics. Now, in Serbia a similar process was beginning. Non-communist parties were in the course of being formed in the summer of 1990, and they were raising the demand that multi-party elections be held in Serbia also. The ruling party in Serbia, the League of Communists of Serbia, was willing to accede to that but first they wanted to amend -- adopt a new constitution for Serbia before the elections were held so that the elections would be held under the new constitution and the elections would be for the bodies that were set up by the new constitution and with the authorities established in the new constitution. This speech is given by Slobodan Milosevic, who was the President of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia to the Serbian assembly in connection with the adoption of a new constitution. The situation in June in that respect was that the League of Communists of Serbia was proposing that a referendum be held in Serbia on the issue of whether the new constitution should be adopted before the elections or after the elections. That referendum, in fact, was held at the end of July and resulted in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We certainly are past the month of June when the speech was given, and his answer was to put the speech in context. Anything then after the speech certainly doesn't give us any context. I also think that there's another difficulty here in the answer to the extent we're talking about putting the speech in context, which is, and I'm referring to line 90, where it indicates -- I'm sorry, page 90, line 2, where Mr. Treanor indicates "the ruling party in Serbia, the League of Communists of Serbia, was willing to accede to that, but first they wanted to ..." and then he discusses amending the constitution. But later on he indicates, and that's on page 90, at line 12 and 13 -- starting at line 10, that "the situation in June in that respect was that the League of Communists in Serbia was proposing that a referendum be held on the issue of whether the new constitution be adopted." So I'm not sure whether or not he's speaking from a standpoint of contextually of, in fact, what was occurring with the League of Communists at that time. And rather than go through, I think, a rather arduous or torturous process of cross-examination with this kind of particular detail, since he is, for purposes of discussion, dealing with the context of a speech, I would appreciate it if rather than put value - which is what he's doing now, he's making subjective value judgements with regard to what was occurring - he gives us the context, meaning the factual information, that was present at the time, which he obviously received from those documents that he specifically chose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the referendum is part of the context of the speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can ask Mr. Treanor, can you tell the Court what Belgrade's position was to the breakup of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we can go to the speech now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have been asked a question now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, he's going to answer the question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the speech Slobodan Milosevic sets out certain positions in regard to the issue of the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, which is -- forms the subject of the passages that we've selected to -- I've selected to focus on here. I'm not sure how to direct you to the proper --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can blow up what is on the second column, above the bullet point in the B/C/S, and then on page 3 of the English translation, starting with the text "That is why this draft on the constitution of Serbia has been prepared ..."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: The portion I would like to focus on is further down in this column, toward the bottom, in which Slobodan Milosevic notes that basically that if the SFRY were to be changed into a confederation as opposed to a federation, then the issue of the borders of the republics of the federation would be opened. He says that he does not consider a confederation to be a state and that therefore the borders of the republics cannot be changed into -- cannot remain as borders if the federation were to cease to be a federation and become a confederation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: And he concludes in the next column by saying that if that were to happen, the question of the borders of Serbia would then become an open political question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's on page 4 of the transcript -- the English translation, I'm sorry. Did the idea of assisting Serbs outside of Serbia find any additional expression at that time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, it finds expression elsewhere in this document. If we can move over to the next column, the last column on the extreme right, and blow that up. In that portion he notes that the -- the Serbia that will be established under the new constitution, which will be a unitary state, a unitary state of Serbia, meaning that it will -- the government of Serbia will have power throughout the territory of Serbia, whereas previously there had been two autonomous provinces in Serbia, Kosovo and Vojvodina, which had extensive powers. Those have been eliminated -- actually, they had been eliminated by constitutional amendment previously, and that situation would be enshrined in the new constitution as well. He says that this new unitary Serbia will be in a position to defend the interests of Serbs outside of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And does this idea of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't know whether at this point, and this is whether or not Mr. Treanor is reading from the original as he interprets it, but if I'm following his response, he is referring to the second full sentence which I read in English as not that this new unitary Serbia will be in a position to defend the position to defend the interests of Serbs outside of Serbia, but rather that Serbia will at the same time be certain guarantee for protection of the interests of Serbian people who live out of Serbia. And that's quite a different statement from that which Mr. Treanor has suggested. I don't know if that's occurred because he was reading from the document as he interprets it or whether or not he is being now liberal with the language of Mr. Milosevic's speech. But I think it's kind of important that with regard to the road that we're going down, that we are quite accurate and that we rely upon here the translation as it is set forth, because certainly a position to defend the interests is quite different than a guarantee for protection of the interests, and it embodies a series of not only political but social principles that are distinct from that which I think Mr. Treanor is driving at in his answer. My concern is that we are verbatim accurate in this regard and that we should not -- we should not slip into interpreting that which has been said and been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Treanor does not have to read verbatim the translation. He can put his own opinion to the words that are written on that page. The very fact that certain words are written there doesn't mean that it's true. He can -- he can tell you his interpretation of what that text means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, why should we have this text here? Why doesn't he just close this text and he gives us his opinion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He can do that, but this is to assist Your Honours. This is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when we are going out here to write the judgement and Mr. Treanor is not here, we're going to be looking at this document, we're going to be looking at the transcript, and if we find that there are inconsistencies between what he says and the document, what do you suggest we do?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He's putting his view of what he believes that paragraph means, so it's the weight that you want to give to his testimony. And if my colleague wants to cross-examine him on any of these matters, then he can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think before he gives his opinion, he must tell us the facts first, as they stand, and then he can give his opinion on those facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, did the idea of assisting Serbs outside of Serbia find any additional expression at that time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. At this time, just a few weeks later, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Rule 65 ter number 06739 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we done with the speech?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can go to page 10 of the B/C/S version and page 11 of the English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. A few weeks after the speech in the Serbian assembly that we just saw, the Socialist Party of Serbia was founded. It was founded as an amalgamation of the League of Communists of Serbia and the Socialist Alliance of the Working People of Serbia, which were two preexisting political institutions from the SFRY. At the founding congress on the 16th of July, 1990, the party adopted a programme, a rather extensive programme covering all sorts of social, economic, and political issues. And we find in the programme points that deal with the Serbs outside of Serbia. At the top of the page, I would like to draw your attention to that passage, Your Honours. At this point I'm -- I must admit I'm a little bit confused as to what you want me to do, whether to summarize the passage or to give it my own translation. I have been in other courtrooms and different Trial Chambers have adopted different approaches to that, so I'd appreciate guidance as to your approach. In considering that issue, I would venture that the report I've written and the testimony I'm given -- I'm giving is mine. It's my report and my testimony. I have, as I mentioned, been through this process before, and I'm aware that the translations that are provided are often inaccurate and need correction on the one hand, and on the other, of course what you are offered in the report and my testimony is my understanding of the documents rather than the understanding of a translator, however good the translation may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The short answer is do what your counsel asks you to do. We can't prescribe to you what to do. And if what you do is found unacceptable by your counsel's opposite number, he will rise onto his feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, just touching on the translations, if you will, for a moment, and you said that sometimes they are incorrect. Is it the case that in this institution, due to the limited resources from CLSS, that the Office of the Prosecutor has draft translations done from a certain unit and that those translations are then submitted into the court, and unless either of the parties find discrepancies with those translations, then they can be admitted into the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that -- the answer to that question may certainly be well outside the purview of this particular witness's knowledge. That is a matter that exists as between the parties themselves and is -- with regard to that, it's one of a number of solutions that have been found. But it, many times, depends on the importance and critical nature of the translations that exist, whereas here the witness has indicated there are inaccuracies, and we do not know what those inaccuracies are, and if the Prosecution is inviting me at this point in time to wholesale make such an agreement with them, I respectfully decline because of the important nature of the words that have been translated and the meaning that is going to be given to those words by this Chamber as a result of how this witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I certainly wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- I wasn't asking my friend to concede anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was simply making a distinction that there are differences of translations. Some are in final form and some are in draft form. If I can move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be of some guidance, then, with regard to the exercise that we're engaged in right now whether we're dealing with draft translations or final translations and what we are going to do in the future with regard to the import of this information, which is independent of the issue of the witness's offer to operate, as I understand it, at least in some regards, as a summary witness, which raises other legal considerations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He's not being offered as a summary witness. He's giving his opinion as to what this document states. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem, and the problem I have is -- I have it with both counsel. You put the proposition, Madam Sutherland, to the witness that, due to the limited resources in CLSS, the Office of the Prosecutor has drafted translations done from a certain unit and that those translations are then submitted into court. Mr. Guy-Smith says that that is a matter that exists as between the parties themselves and is with regards to that, it's one of a number of solutions that have been found. I'm left with the impression that the parties are agreed that some translations were not translated by official Tribunal translators. Is that understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is my understanding as of now. In this session I now understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that is a position that is held by both parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Being in court today, I now understand that we do not have official translations with regard to all documents that are being presented to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before this session, I would not have been able to say that. That's something I learned in the course of what's going on here. Perhaps I made an assumption --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, from --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I assist please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This has been going on in this institution for a number of years, and it is quite easy to work out whether it's a CLSS translation or it's done by a unit within the Office of the Prosecutor. If it's done within the Office of the Prosecutor, it will have the words "ET" before the translation number at the top of the page, or it, in fact, says "Draft Translation." If it's done by CLSS, then it's a revised translation, and it has the words -- or it may, in fact, even be a draft translation done by the CLSS, but it has the words "EDT" at the end of the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. That may very well be so, ma'am. It hasn't happened in this chamber. Let me come back to you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I don't understand you. Your statement to the effect that it's one of a number of solutions that have been found, and this solution has been found as between the parties, like you said, that suggests you had prior knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do -- I do apologise for not being more specific. The reference that I am making there is to the prior trials that I have been involved in where there has been a draft translation or there has been another document and the Prosecutor has offered the draft translation as being the document upon which we could rely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- and I have said -- I have said both yes and no. That's what I meant by "the agreement between the parties." So that when we come to the Chamber, we say, as the Chamber has said to us on occasion, This is a draft translation; are the parties comfortable with it? And we have said yes, and we have said no. That's what I meant by that. Not with regard to this particular case. That issue never came up. We have never had that discussion, and I did not consider that we would be having a translation discussion. I didn't -- I didn't consider we'd be in that world with this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, can we get on to the same page. We are not discussing other cases, we are discussing this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if what you're referring to relates to other cases, then that's not what we are talking about. We are talking about this case. And the language that you use relating to that -- to the fact that you say that that is a matter that exists as between the parties themselves, which parties are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this specific case, I clearly used a language that was inexact and inappropriate, and I apologise to the Chamber for doing that, because with regard to this particular case there is nothing that exists between the parties with regard to this issue. Nothing. So to the extent that I used inexact language, let me be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you sit down and before I hand over to Madam Sutherland, what, then, do you suggest be done with this translation that is apparently not by a qualified CLSS employee?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this point my concern is that this translation is now going to be interpreted by the witness, thereby removing us further from potentially what actually was said in the original document, and that is something that I would object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's about as far as I can go for the moment because thus far what we have experienced is the presentation of a document in the original language and in English and then a factual recitation of what that document says by the witness, which is already distinct from the specific language that exists in English. So I have -- since I think we're at a point where a number of these words are going to have great intent, and by "intent" I mean meaning, with regard to some kind of fundamental issues that exist in this case, I have grave concerns about operating on the basis of a translation that is, as the witness has said, inaccurate, upon which he is now going to render an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Treanor didn't say that this translation was inaccurate. He was making --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's right. I was not referring to this particular document. I was speaking in general. Again, if I can explain my work, perhaps, in more detail. We discussed earlier at some length the process of review and selection of documents. I do that, and the people that work for me do that, working with the original documents. We don't work from translations. Why don't we work from translations? Well, first of all, we don't need to. Second of all, typically, the documents that we're working with haven't been translated yet. When I wrote this report, very many of those documents had not been translated. I'm not sure which ones were, which ones weren't, but I know that recently there's been quite a push put on to get documents in the report -- that are mentioned in the report, used in the report, translated. So I infer from that that many of them were not translated. Again, that doesn't bother me because I don't use the translations, I use the original documents. And as I indicated before, what I offer in the report and what I seek to offer the Court now is the meaning of these documents to me and not the meaning that those documents may have to someone else. I'm not calling into question any particular translation, and not this one which, by the way, appears to be the official SPS translation of the document, although I'm not a hundred per cent certain of that. But that's what it appears to be. It's just that in my experience, I have run into occasions where the translations that were offered were, in fact, incomplete and inaccurate. So I -- which is just another reason for me to not to be bothered with translations at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I heard you say at the beginning of your testimony, Mr. Treanor, that you have - excuse me - a basic reading knowledge of the language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Basic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I said "basic." I believe I said I had a very good reading knowledge of the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think you said "good" either. I'm clearly left with the impression that it was not a good knowledge. I don't know the line and the page, but that's the impression I was left with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, how long have you been reading the B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Approximately 35 years. I've been using it in my research, in my official capacity, and as a translator for about that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anyway, Madam Sutherland, you have an objection from your learned friend. Any response to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've lost it on the page, and I don't recall it. If you could summarize it for me, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith said if we are using unofficially translated documents which may, in fact, be inaccurate and then we still get a personal opinion of the witness on them, we're moving further away from what the original document said and on that basis, he would object.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's two issues there. The first one is on unofficial translated documents. Mr. Guy-Smith has just come onto this case, but this case has been dealing for a long time with draft translations, and that's just the nature of the beast. We have in this institution eight trials running simultaneously, or we're supposed to be having eight trials running simultaneously. CLSS do not have the resources to translate thousands and thousands and thousands of pages of documents in relation to those trials. And so we have to, everybody has to rely on the draft translations that have been done by CLSS because they haven't -- they don't have the resources to revise them before we need to use them in the courtroom, or the other department that does the draft -- that does the unofficial translations. And it's been the practice for quite a number of years that those translations are accepted into the court unless the parties object to them, and then they are sent for revision. But if there's no objection, then those draft unofficial translations are accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do have an objection to them, number one, ma'am, number two, and that's what we discussed, the objection to using them. And number two --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can just touch on the second issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just finish with what you've told us. You say it's been a number of years. How long have we been having eight cases running at the same time? Is it a number of years?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At least four years, maybe three years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Eight cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, don't quote me on it. I know that for at least two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And because of that are you saying we should run the risk of unfair proceedings because of likely mistakes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just said unless the Defence objects to a document, if they don't object -- it's not unfair to the accused, if the Defence don't have a problem with the translation. This institution would come to a grinding halt if we had to get a revised CLSS translation of every single document that we seek to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that indeed it may happen that the opposite number doesn't object, but that does not remove the fact that if indeed the inaccuracy has slipped the attention of the opposite side or he has no way of finding out whether it is an inaccurate and it does slip in, then there is unfairness either to the Prosecution or to the Defence, and that is why CLSS was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: CLSS have a very limited number of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The completion strategy, we would still be here in 2020 if we had to wait for the translation of the number of pages that are going through the courts at the moment. And a lot of these bigger cases are so document heavy, as opposed to where you may have one accused from Prijedor in a camp case, as opposed to the leadership cases where they are very document oriented. I mean, that's the -- that's the reality, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that your response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, unless the Defence object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought they said they're objecting. You asked me to summarize what the objection was, and I told you -- I summarized it for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I understand Mr. Guy-Smith well, he's now saying he's objecting to the draft translation of any document we seek to tender? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to clarify yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to those documents that Mr. Treanor is using which are draft translations, in the absence of information at the present time concerning the accuracy of those translations, we object. With regard to any other witness, we may reach a different point depending on who the witness is and what the import is of those translations. But given the experience that we have had thus far in a very limited period of time concerning the issue not only of translation but also his interpretation of what is being said, we have no alternative but at this point to object because we are concerned that we will not be dealing accurately with the information that's contained therein and cannot intelligently respond thereto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just briefly say that we've been disclosing a lot of documents over a number of years, and we advised the Defence that they have a number of Serbo-Croat readers on their team. If they have any objection to the documents, then one would assume that they would bring them up with us before now, instead of at the moment the witness is testifying. But if I can say, Your Honour, if we can address this issue with you in court tomorrow, we would prefer to do that, the whole translation issue of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're expanding the problem. At this stage we're dealing with this document before us. If, however, you do want to talk about the whole issue of translation, you're welcome to do so at an opportune moment. Bear in mind that at this stage you have an objection in your hands, and it is no answer to that objection to refer to the translations that have been done over the years. I would like a response that is focused on what is before us right now. I note the time. You might perhaps want to respond to this objection, pertinently to what we are doing now, tomorrow. You're welcome to do so. And then if you want to expand the document to all translations, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take you up on your offer to go into the matter tomorrow and answer the objection. Just on one matter, though. In relation to Mr. Treanor's proficiency, I would just direct Your Honours to page 74 of the LiveNote, lines 12 to 16, that is, his reading proficiency in the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 74? Line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies to you, Mr. Treanor. My apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you for your apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland, would this then be an opportune moment?

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, given the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Court adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00. Same courtroom. Court adjourned. You do know, Mr. Treanor, that being in this witness stand, you don't have to talk to anybody. You don't need to be told this, in any case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.
